STEP 1 - Scene: Two pieces of cooked sweet corn (corn on the cob, cut into rounds) on a white triangular/rounded plate, photographed from above at a slight angle. Only the corn is part of this meal; the white bowl at the bottom right is not food.

STEP 2 - Ruler: The plate is roughly a dinner-plate size, about 26 cm across its longest undistorted width. Area ≈ 3.14 × (13)² ≈ 530 cm², though the triangular shape is smaller in usable area, so I estimate the plate's usable food area at about 400 cm².

STEP 3 - Items: Two corn cob rounds (one larger, one smaller), cooked yellow sweet corn with the kernels visible, no visible butter or sauce.

STEP 4 - Area: The larger round covers about 60 cm² of the plate (roughly 15%), the smaller round about 40 cm² (roughly 10%). Together ~25% of the plate.

STEP 5 - Volume: Each round is a cylinder-like piece about 3.5–4 cm in diameter and about 3–3.5 cm thick, so each is roughly 35–40 ml. Using the visible footprint and height: large piece ≈ 60 cm² × 3.5 cm ≈ 210 ml envelope; small piece ≈ 40 cm² × 3 cm ≈ 120 ml. Since the corn is a hollow-cored cob with kernels, I take the solid volume at roughly 60% of the envelope: about 125 ml + 70 ml ≈ 195 ml total.

STEP 6 - Grams: Cooked corn kernels on cob have a bulk density near 0.7–0.8 g/ml when treated as cut vegetable pieces, but the cob core is dense, so I use 0.7 g/ml: 195 ml × 0.7 ≈ 137 g.

STEP 7 - Energy: Cooked sweet corn on the cob is about 96 kcal per 100 g (cooked, kernels with cob core included in the weight estimate; the cob itself is largely inedible, so I apply the kernel-value figure of about 90 kcal/100 g to the edible portion). Using 137 g × 90 kcal/100 g ≈ 123 kcal.

STEP 8 - Sanity check: Two corn rounds of this size (roughly two medium-to-large cob sections) is plausible at about 130–140 g total and roughly 120 kcal. This is consistent with what is visible on a large plate with modest food coverage.
